In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and functional characterization of a novel class of proteins involved in regulation of antibiotic biosynthesis in actinomycetes.
the function of STPs in S. coeliacolor, which are the first to be described in this organism.
a better understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of STPKs in actinobacterial cells, and the potential of manipulating these mechanisms to improve antibiotic production.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PknB is a serine/threonin protein kinase that phosphorylates a number of target proteins and that FHA proteins are potential targets for this kinase.
FHA‐STPK signalling pathways in Streptomyce are complex and that their role in regulating central metabolism may vary between species.
FHA proteins in S. coeliacolor act as negative regulators of PknB signalling and that this signalling pathway has a key role in the control of carbon flux to antibiotic biosynthesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the FHA‐PknB module in S. coeliacolor has a regulatory role in central carbon metabolism and that this pathway is a potential target for metabolic engineering.
the PknB‐FhaAB signalling pathway regulates the flux of carbon towards actinorhodins in S. coeliacolor, and this is likely to be mediated by a yet unidentified factor.
PknB is not essential, but is a potential regulator of central carbon metabolism and antibiotic production, with FhaAB as candidate interacting partners.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the function of PknB is modulated by FhaAB, which in turn can be modulated by other factors.
the FHA domain protein FhaA can act as a negative regulator of PknB‐driven antibiotic production.
the function of PknB in S.coelicolor is not related to the control of cell shape.
